'''''Nicotiana quadrivalvis''''' is a species of [[Nicotiana|wild tobacco]] known as '''Indian tobacco'''. The variety ''N. quadrivalvis'' var. ''multivalvis'' is known by the common name '''Columbian tobacco'''.<ref name="bull" /> It is endemic to the western United States, where it grows in many types of habitat. It is a bushy, sprawling annual herb growing up to two meters in maximum height. The lower leaf blades are up to {{convert|15|cm|in|0}} long and are borne on short [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]], the upper smaller and sessile on the stem. The [[inflorescence]] is an array of several white, greenish, or purple-tinged flowers with tubular throats up to 5 centimeters long. The base of each is enclosed in a ridged calyx of [[sepal]]s. The flower face may be {{convert|5|cm|in|0}} wide. The fruit is a capsule up to {{convert|2|cm|in|frac=4}} in length.

It is also called "'''sacred tobacco''',"<ref name="Traditional Use of Tobacco among Indigenous Peoples of North America">{{Cite web |url=https://cottfn.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/TUT-Literature-Review.pdf |title=Traditional Use of Tobacco among Indigenous Peoples of North America |last=Tonio |first=Sadik |date=March 28, 2014}}</ref>  by different [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] cultures. ''[[Nicotiana rustica]]'' can also be considered sacred.<ref name="Holy Smoke: Tobacco Use Among Native American Tribes in North America">{{Cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Nicotiana-rustica_fig1_233422262 |title=Holy Smoke: Tobacco Use Among Native American Tribes in North America |last=Godlaski |first=Theodore M |date=November 2012 |access-date=2019-12-28}}</ref><ref name="Walking towards the sacred">{{Cite web |url=http://www.glitc.org/forms/Tabacco/tabacco-booklet-web-.pdf |title=Walking towards the sacred |last=Brokenleg |first=Isaiah |website=glitc.org |access-date=2019-12-28}}</ref><ref name="Harrod1992">{{cite book|author=Howard L. Harrod|title=Renewing the World: Plains Indian Religion and Morality|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JiRhC2UTDWcC&pg=PA182|date=February 1992|publisher=University of Arizona Press|isbn=978-0-8165-1312-3|pages=182–}}</ref><ref name="Aboriginal Tobaccos">{{Cite journal |title=Aboriginal Tobaccos |last=Setchell |first=William Albert |journal = American Anthropologist|year = 1921|volume = 23|issue = 4|pages = 397–414|doi = 10.1525/aa.1921.23.4.02a00020|jstor = 660667|url = https://zenodo.org/record/1641080|doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name="Biomolecular archaeology reveals ancient origins of indigenous tobacco smoking in North American Plateau">{{Cite journal |url=https://www.pnas.org/content/pnas/early/2018/10/23/1813796115.full.pdf |title=Biomolecular archaeology reveals ancient origins of indigenous tobacco smoking in North American Plateau |last=Tushingham |first=Shannon |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=September 26, 2018 |volume=115 |issue=46 |pages=11742–11747 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1813796115 |pmid=30373836 |pmc=6243282 |access-date=2019-12-28 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018PNAS..11511742T }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Nicotiana quadrivalvis'' has traditionally been cultivated by [[indigenous peoples]] living on the west coast of the United States, primarily in particular southern [[Oregon]] and northern [[California]], and along the middle [[Columbia River]]. Individually owned plots of tobacco plants were seeded with the previous year's seed capsules, tilled and weeded and fertilized in the fall by mixing in rotten wood after the harvest. The species was first described from the upper [[Missouri River]] where it was cultivated by the [[Mandan]] and [[Arikara]]. <ref>Pursh. Flora Americae Septentrionalis. 1814.[https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/396556]</ref>

Further north, the [[Haida people|Haida]], [[Tlingit people|Tlingit]], and probably [[Tsimshian]] cultivate a related variety of tobacco long thought to have gone extinct, ''Nicotiana quadrivalvis'' var. ''multivalvis'', in a similar manner. The original seeds must have been acquired from afar, as tobacco was not native to the northern [[Pacific Northwest|Northwest Coast]]. [[Native American mythology|Myths]] reflecting this describe the supernatural original acquisition of the seeds.<ref>Deur, Douglas and Turner, Nancy J. ''Keeping it Living''. University of Washington Press, 2005, p. 13.</ref>

Seeds of var. ''multivalvis'' were brought to London by botanist [[David Douglas (botanist)|David Douglas]], having stolen them at night in 1825. The seeds found themselves in a seed bank in [[Puławy]], Poland where they were returned to the [[Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians]].<ref name="bull">{{cite news |last1=Bull |first1=Brian |title=Once thought lost for good, Native Americans' prized tobacco is back in Oregon |url=https://www.klcc.org/arts-culture/2023-11-20/once-thought-lost-for-good-native-americans-prized-tobacco-is-back-in-oregon |access-date=21 November 2023 |work=KLCC {{!}} NPR for Oregonians |publisher=National Public Radio |date=20 November 2023 |language=en}}</ref>
